strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem at the intersection of continual learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL), where coordination conventions and non-stationarity make retention uniquely challenging.

The JAX-based end-to-end GPU implementation provides substantial speedups over standard CPU-based RL environments, making it feasible to train across long task sequences (20–100 tasks) on modest hardware within hours.
The procedural layout generator and deterministic reachability/solvability validator are well-designed and thoroughly detailed, guaranteeing solvable kitchens with controllable difficulty.

Provides a comprehensive set of baseline evaluations and ablations (multi-head vs. single head, task conditioning, layer norm, critic regularization, network capacity/plasticity loss) that yield practical insights for CMARL architectures.
weaknesses: The benchmark is currently restricted to a single domain (two-player Overcooked) with fully observable, discrete grid environments. While procedural generation offers spatial variety, it lacks diversity in task dynamics, agent counts, partial observability, or competitive/mixed-motive scenarios.

The evaluated continual learning methods are limited primarily to classic parameter-regularization baselines (EWC, Online EWC, MAS, L2). Important families of CRL approaches—such as experience replay, distillation-based methods, or recent continual MARL techniques (e.g., progressive task contextualization)—are not evaluated.

The bulk of the empirical results and ablations focus on Level 1 (easy) tasks. As shown in Figure 7, baseline performance collapses substantially on Level 2 and Level 3 environments, but the paper offers limited analysis or algorithmic remedies for why existing methods fail so severely on higher difficulty tiers.

Strong performance heavily depends on task-incremental multi-head architectures (as shown in the ablation where removing multi-head collapses score to near zero), which limits applicability in more realistic continual settings where task identity is unavailable or task boundaries are fuzzy.

strengths: High computational throughput: Implementing the benchmark and training pipeline end-to-end in JAX significantly reduces the wall-clock time required for long-sequence continual reinforcement learning (training a 20-task sequence within hours on a single GPU), which alleviates a major computational bottleneck in CRL research.

Procedural layout generation with solvability guarantees: The procedural generation pipeline paired with a multi-step graph reachability validator (Appendix A.2 and A.3) provides an infinite stream of verified, solvable cooperative layouts across three explicit difficulty levels.

Comprehensive empirical investigation of plasticity and ablations: The manuscript not only tracks standard CRL metrics (average performance, forgetting, plasticity) across multiple baseline methods, but also includes insightful ablations (Figure 5) and an empirical study of plasticity loss over repeated task sequences (Figure 6, Table 3).
weaknesses: Narrow domain and MARL scope: Despite the benchmark being framed for Continual Multi-Agent RL generally, it is strictly restricted to 2-agent, fully observable, symmetric Overcooked grid environments. Key challenges distinctive to MARL—such as partial observability, asymmetric roles/capabilities, scaling beyond 2 agents, communication protocols, and non-stationarity from changing partner policies—are not explored.

Limited algorithmic novelty and exploration: The paper is purely a benchmarking effort that combines standard IPPO with off-the-shelf single-agent continual learning regularizers (EWC, MAS, L2). No specialized CMARL method or mechanism addressing multi-agent coordination retention is proposed.

Evaluation restricted to a single base MARL algorithm: Experiments exclusively evaluate IPPO. Popular cooperative MARL paradigms such as value factorization methods (e.g., QMIX, VDN) or centralized training with decentralized execution (MAPPO) are not benchmarked, leaving it unclear how value-based or centralized critic methods interact with continual learning.

Heavily reliant on task-incremental multi-head separation: The ablation study (Figure 5) reveals that performance across all methods collapses completely without separate task-specific policy heads ('No Multihead'). This indicates that the setup heavily leans on oracle task segmentation rather than truly shared continuous representation learning, sidestepping key representation-sharing challenges in continual learning.

strengths: GPU-Accelerated Efficiency: Implementing the benchmark entirely in JAX enables end-to-end vectorization on the GPU, drastically cutting training wall-clock time (e.g., training across 20 tasks in a few hours on a single GPU) and overcoming the throughput limitations of traditional CPU-bound continual RL benchmarks.

Procedural Generation with Formal Verification: The procedural kitchen generator combined with an automated reachability and solvability validator (Appendix A.2 and A.3) provides a mathematically grounded, infinite stream of valid tasks across defined difficulty tiers.

Principled Normalization Metric: Deriving an analytical upper-bound baseline based on single-agent shortest-path cook-deliver cycles enables standardized and interpretable performance tracking across heterogeneous layouts.

Insightful Empirical Ablations: The ablation studies and plasticity experiments (analyzing multi-head heads, layer normalization, CNN vs. MLP encoders, and capacity loss under repeated sequences) provide actionable insights into architectural prerequisites for continual learning in grid-based environments.
weaknesses: Conceptual Inconsistency Regarding Task Incremental Evaluation: In Section 3 ('Continual MARL'), the paper defines the setup as: 'the task-incremental setting, where the task identity is known during training but hidden at evaluation.' In standard continual learning terminology, task identity hidden at test time corresponds to domain-incremental or class-incremental learning. More critically, the default models rely on multi-head architectures where a specific task head is chosen; selecting this head at evaluation requires the task ID, which directly contradicts the claim that task identity is hidden at test time.

Narrow Multi-Agent Scope: Although positioned as a continual multi-agent benchmark, the setup is restricted to two agents with full observability, homogeneous shared policies (IPPO), and fixed co-players. Many core challenges unique to continual MARL—such as partial observability (Dec-POMDP), non-stationary partner policies, role divergence, and ad-hoc team play—are largely absent, making the benchmark behave closely to single-agent gridworld control with two bodies.

Limited Domain Diversity: The benchmark is confined strictly to Overcooked mechanics (soup preparation, carrying onions, plates, pots). While spatial layout diversity is high, the underlying dynamics, action spaces, and reward structure remain uniform across all tasks.

Omission of MARL-Specific Continual Learning Baselines: The evaluated baselines are standard single-agent continual learning regularizers (FT, L2, EWC, Online EWC, MAS) mapped onto IPPO. While these are foundational, recent continual MARL techniques (e.g., progressive task contextualization by Yuan et al., 2024, or multi-agent replay/distillation strategies) are not benchmarked.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored research area at the intersection of continual learning and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL), where non-stationarity arises simultaneously from changing task distributions and co-adapting teammates.

Excellent computational throughput achieved via an end-to-end JAX implementation, enabling training across long task sequences (20+ tasks, reaching billions of environment steps for plasticity evaluations) on a single commodity GPU in just a few hours.

Well-designed procedural generation pipeline equipped with a rigorous 10-rule deterministic graph-reachability validator to ensure all generated layouts are solvable and promote coordination or item hand-offs.

Comprehensive empirical investigation evaluating six established CL baselines across multiple difficulty levels, supported by extensive analyses including network plasticity degradation, architectural ablations (highlighting the critical role of multi-head structures), agent scaling (N=1, 2, 3), partial observability, and role heterogeneity.
weaknesses: Domain diversity is limited to variants of Overcooked. Although the procedural generator alters layouts, obstacle densities, roles, and observability windows, the fundamental mechanics (collect onions, cook in pot, plate, and deliver) remain identical across tasks, lacking cross-domain heterogeneity.

Evaluations are largely restricted to the task-incremental CL paradigm utilizing multi-head architectures with known task boundaries, which sidesteps harder domain-incremental or task-agnostic settings where agents must operate without task identity oracle signals.

MARL baseline selection is relatively narrow, focusing almost exclusively on IPPO (with a brief evaluation of MAPPO in the partially observable setting), omitting other major cooperative paradigms such as value-factorization methods (e.g., QMIX/VDN) or learned communication protocols.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored niche: Continual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (CMARL), where the dual challenges of non-stationarity and catastrophic forgetting intersect.

The framework is fully implemented in JAX, providing GPU-accelerated environment simulation and training that allows long task sequences (up to 100 tasks) to be trained in a few hours on a standard desktop setup.
Includes a robust procedural generation pipeline paired with a deterministic BFS/DFS validator to guarantee solvability and reachability for all generated layouts across multiple difficulty tiers.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation exploring multiple orthogonal dimensions: architectural choices (multi-head, layer norm, CNN vs. MLP), plasticity loss, agent scaling (1–3 agents), reward structures (shared, individual, sparse), partial observability, and designated heterogeneous roles.
weaknesses: Environment scope is confined to a single domain: Although procedural layout variation provides diversity in geometry and routing, all tasks share identical underlying Overcooked mechanics (chopping/fetching onions, cooking, plating, delivering), limiting the benchmark's generalizability across diverse cooperative dynamics.

Heavy reliance on oracle task IDs and multi-head architectures: The ablation shows that removing task-specific heads causes catastrophic collapse, meaning current baseline success relies heavily on task-incremental isolation rather than learning unified shared representations across tasks.

Lack of domain-specific CMARL baselines: The evaluated methods are standard single-agent CL algorithms (EWC, MAS, L2, AGEM) combined naively with IPPO/MAPPO; existing specialized continual multi-agent approaches (e.g., progressive contextualization methods cited in related work) are not evaluated as baselines.

Low baseline performance on harder layouts: On Level 3 tasks, almost all baseline methods achieve very low average scores (below 0.3 normalized score) and negative forward transfer, showing that naive CL+MARL combinations fail to make meaningful progress on complex coordination challenges.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem at the intersection of continual learning (CL) and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where non-stationarity arises from both changing tasks and shifting teammate policies.

End-to-end GPU acceleration via JAX provides exceptional throughput, overcoming the major computational bottleneck of CPU-bound CL benchmarks and enabling fast experimentation over long task sequences (up to 100 tasks) on modest hardware.

Careful procedural environment generation with a formal 10-rule solvability and reachability validator, paired with an analytical single-agent upper bound for fair score normalization across varying layout topologies.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation spanning six CL baselines across three difficulty tiers, backed by informative ablations (multi-head architectures, encoder types, LayerNorm, task IDs), plasticity loss investigations, reward structure variations, and partial observability studies.

Provides valuable empirical takeaways, notably the critical role of multi-head architectures in CMARL, the unexpected failure of centralized critics (MAPPO) under task drift, and the degradation of continual learning performance when moving beyond two agents.
weaknesses: Domain breadth is restricted to a single environment family (Overcooked gridworld). While layout variation is rich, Overcooked has specific discrete mechanics that may not reflect continuous control, complex physics, competitive dynamics, or long-horizon strategic coordination found in other MARL benchmarks.

Heavy reliance on the task-incremental paradigm with known task boundaries and multi-head heads. As demonstrated in the ablation, removing the multi-head structure severely degrades performance, leaving open how these findings translate to task-agnostic, task-free, or domain-incremental continual MARL settings.

Algorithm diversity on the MARL side is narrow: experiments almost exclusively rely on IPPO (with a brief comparison to MAPPO under partial observability). Standard cooperative value-factorization methods (such as QMIX or VDN) or off-policy actor-critic approaches are omitted.
